en: Peṭakopadesa 5.
The Fifth Stage: The Analysis of the Modes of Conveying.
Therein, what is the analysis of the modes of conveying?
Wherein the sixteen modes of conveyance (hāra) reach their differentiation through the flavor of the syllables (akkharaso):
therein, at the beginning, is the mode of conveyance of the teaching (desanāhāra).
Therein, this verse is either wholesome or unwholesome, or it concerns the Truths (sacca) or a portion of the Truths.
What is taught?
In the Sutta, the "nourishment of investigation" is taught.
For example, regarding the Noble Truths: the presentation consists of the four truths, both common and uncommon.

And as for the eighteen terms, they are suffering in seven ways: briefly, by way of bodily and mental suffering, by association with the unpleasant, by dissociation from the pleasant, and by the three characteristics of the conditioned.
Therein, the three characteristics of the conditioned are the three kinds of suffering: arising is a characteristic of the conditioned, and it is suffering through the suffering of formations;
change is a characteristic of the conditioned, and it is suffering through the suffering of change; and alteration is a characteristic of the conditioned.

The suffering of suffering is a state of suffering; among these three characteristics of the conditioned, in the three planes of feeling, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is the characteristic of arising, and it is a state of suffering due to the suffering of formations.
Furthermore, pleasant feeling is a state of suffering due to the suffering of formations and the suffering of change, which is its alteration.
The characteristic of the conditioned (*saṅkhatalakkhaṇa*), painful feeling (*dukkhā vedanā*), and the suffering of suffering (*dukkhadukkhatā*)—
these forms of suffering are to be sought within these nine terms, specifically within the first seven and the sixteen terms; furthermore,
eleven characteristics of suffering have been explained in the *Niddesa*.
Birth has the characteristic of manifestation, and death has the characteristic of the passing away of what has manifested; thus, fifteen terms should be elaborated in detail.

In this way, there are fifty [terms]—both common and uncommon—within the seven and ten bases, within the threefold *Sāsanappaṭṭhāna*, within the eighteenfold *suttādhiṭṭhāna*s, and within the tenfold *suttavidheyya*s.
Among the sixteen modes of conveying the teaching (*hāra*) and the twenty-one kinds of investigative analysis (*pavicaya-vīmaṃsā*), this has been taught.
And because it is taught according to reality, this is called the "mode of conveying the teaching" (*desanā-hāra*).
In that regard, what is the "mode of conveying analysis" (*vicaya-hāra*)?
“Footstep, question, and inquiry:
what is first and what is last?
The chant and its analysis.”
"The string is defined as 'investigation' (vicaya).
The word 'padam' means the first word.
What is its meaning?"

That which was asked by the Venerable Ajita when the Blessed One was questioned is what should be grasped. As for the few words asked, such as the verse beginning, “By what is the world shut in?”—these four words constitute the question for the answer.
And as for the extent to which those words were answered by the Blessed One, that elucidation of the words constitutes the question; this is called a "word.
These four words are the "questions."
How many questions are there?
One, two, or more than that—these four phrases constitute one question; the phrasing follows the meaning, and even many phrases may ask about only a single meaning.
These four recurring phrases constitute a single question by way of their expression.
"By what is the world enveloped?"—he asks this with reference to the world. "By what does it not shine? What do you say is its defilement?"—he asks that very same thing.
"What is its great fear?"—he asks that very same thing.

Thus, the phrasing follows the meaning; there is one question, and that question is fourfold: that which is to be answered categorically, that which is to be answered analytically, that which is to be answered with a counter-question, and that which is to be set aside.
In this regard, "The eye is impermanent" is to be answered categorically. "That which is impermanent is suffering" is to be answered by way of analysis;
for while there may be things that are impermanent but not the eye, and those sense bases which are not the eye are also impermanent, it is not only the eye [that is so characterized].
This is to be answered by way of analysis. "Is that which is the eye the eye-faculty? is to be answered by way of counter-question.
"That eye is the Tathāgata" is to be set aside;
"other than the eye" is a question to be set aside.
Regarding this question, what was asked by the Blessed One? The defilement of the world was asked about.
What is the reason?
For defilement is threefold: the defilement of craving, the defilement of views, and the defilement of misconduct.
In this context, "enveloped by ignorance" indicates ignorance; "longing" indicates craving; and "great fear" indicates unwholesome [states].
The Blessed One answers: "He shows the ripening of karma; it is impossible that there should be a ripening of suffering to be felt from karma that is to be felt as pleasant—this state does not exist.
Thus it is said: "The world is shrouded by ignorance... and so forth, in four phrases.
Beyond that, he asks in return with the verse, “The streams flow everywhere,” and he asks about four lines which the Blessed One answers with two lines:
“Whatever streams there are in the world,
mindfulness is their damming.”
“I call it the restraint of the streams;
by means of wisdom, these are closed off.
These four lines he answers with two lines.

When asked, “What is this ‘footprint’? he is asked about the cleansing of that defiled world. By the expression “the six streams,” the six groups of craving are indicated with reference to all the sense bases (*āyatana*).
When asked, “By what are those streams blocked? he asks about the abandonment of the obsessions (*pariyuṭṭhāna*); when asked, “By what are the streams covered?

he asks about the uprooting of the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*). In this regard, the Blessed One teaches mindfulness at the six doors; for one who dwells with clear comprehension and with mindfulness as a gatekeeper, his faculties become guarded.

In that regard, whatever insight (*vipassanā*) there is for those whose sense-faculties (*indriya*) are guarded, each such insight leads to the absolute abandonment of those respective streams and of that ignorance (*avijjā*) by which the world is shrouded.
Thus, although the streams are closed, he asks further:

"Wisdom (*paññā*) and mindfulness (*sati*)—where does this [craving] for name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) find its pacification? Having approached the Blessed One to ask this, the Blessed One answers these four terms with a single term.
“Regarding this question you asked,
Ajita, I shall explain it to you...
[etc.]”
"By the cessation of consciousness,
herein it is stilled.
By this question, what does he ask?
He asks about the element of nirvana without residue, and the Blessed One answers that regarding the element of nirvana without residue.
Therein, by the first question he asks about defilement;
by the second question he asks about purification.
By the third question, he asks about the element of nibbāna with residue remaining.
By the fourth question, he asks back regarding the element of nibbāna without residue remaining, and asks further beyond that:
"And those who have realized the Dhamma..."
And as for those many trainees here—
being asked, O Wise One, tell me, dear sir, about their conduct.”
He asks these four terms. And what is the meaning of:
"How many questions are there for those who have mastered the Dhamma—the Arahants and those in training (sekkhā)?
What comes first, and what comes after? This is the sense.
In this context, which one does he ask about first, and which one later?
He asks about the Arahant first.

Among the qualities of those in training (*sekkha*), by which term are the Arahants included as "those who have understood the Dhamma" (*saṅkhātadhamma*)? By the term "many" (*puthu*), the trainees (*sekkha*) are included.
"Among them, he who is wise"—with this common phrase, [the interlocutor] questions the Blessed One.
Both the common and the uncommon points should be asked among those questions;
the Blessed One provides the answer to that.
He does not answer what was asked first by answering what was asked later; rather, he answers what was asked first by answering it first. And as for this question:
"What is the conduct of those who are purified and those who are being purified?"—this was asked, and he answered: "One should not covet sensual pleasures."

"May one not be turbid in mind": by this, the Blessed One prohibits the obsessions (*pariyuṭṭhāna*) through applied thought (*vitakka*). However, there are two types of obsession regarding non-turbidity of thought, as explained among the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).
"Skilled in all things" refers to the Arahant.
"By what does one cross the flood?"—these are the four lines of the verse.
There are only four questions.
What is the reason? Because here the phrasing does not follow the meaning as it did in the first set of Ajita’s questions;
there, there were not exclusively many answers for one question, nor was there only one question when there were many, yet he asked them all previously.
It has been answered, as in the fourth answer to Ajita’s questions; herein, one investigates according to reality through the sequence of words of investigation.
Furthermore, regarding that which is asked here, this manner of questioning—in the verse "Tangle within, tangle without"—is to be sought in the answering of what was asked.
"How does he answer, 'The Blessed One'?
He answers with the verse beginning, "A wise man, established in virtue...
Therein, calm (samatha) pertains to the cultivation of the mind, and insight (vipassanā) pertains to the cultivation of wisdom.
In this regard, it is inferred as follows: those phenomena that are abandoned by both serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*) are these "inner tangles" and "outer tangles.
Regarding this, passion (*rāga*) is abandoned by serenity, and ignorance (*avijjā*) by insight.
Passion based on an internal object is an inner tangle; passion based on an external object is an outer tangle.
The personality-view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi) which has the internal as its basis is the inner tangle.

The sixty-one types of speculative views which have the external as their basis are the outer tangle. Whatever view, having the internal as its basis, will be associated with the category of views—this is the tangle.
Likewise, in brief, whatever craving and views have the internal as their basis, this is the inner tangle.
Whatever craving and views have external objects, these are the "external tangle.
Regarding this, there is the verse with which the deities question the Blessed One: “Four-wheeled, nine-gated.
Therein, the Blessed One replies with the verse: “Having cut the thong and the strap. Herein, the Blessed One replies by teaching the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
By this response, the Blessed One is inferred [to have said] that the defilements are to be pointed out here by what was indicated in the preceding verse.
For "four wheels" refers to the four hands and feet;
"nine gates" refers to the nine openings of the body.
"Four wheels" refers to the four types of clinging; with clinging as condition, there is existence; with the cessation of clinging, there is the cessation of existence.
"Nine doors" refers to the nine kinds of conceit; for suffering arises from the class of conceit. There are three triads: [the first] is fullness; the second is connected with the triad;
and the third is lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure.
In this context, "sinew" (naddhi) refers to craving (taṇhā).
"Tendon" (varatta) refers to conceit (māna), as well as desire and greed, which are evil—the passion for the five strands of sensual pleasure.
In this regard, "evil greed" is pointed out as the craving together with its root.
"Craving is rooted in ignorance" means that craving is rooted in ignorance; [it refers to] the abandoning of both craving and views.
Furthermore, whatever other phenomena leading to saṃsāra are joined by way of the "four wheels" and for that same reason, all of them should be demonstrated.
In this regard, this verse-answer accords with the question and its answer.

"Whatever [verse] is recited together with the prose, the grammar, and the chanting—that is called 'investigation' (vicaya)," said the Blessed One. "He chants along with as many words as the Teacher lays down.
"Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu endowed with eight qualities is worthy to go on an errand.
These eight words have been laid down."
With six verses the Blessed One recited in response:
“He who indeed does not tremble upon encountering an assembly of fierce speech;”
He does not omit a word,
nor does he conceal the teaching;
he speaks without ambiguity.
When questioned, he does not become agitated;
such a bhikkhu indeed is worthy of going on an errand.
In that regard, however, for as many words as the Blessed One deposits, he chants along with that many.
"Endowed with seven factors, monks, a good friend is dear and worthy of veneration"—this, in detail, the Blessed One chants along with seven words.

Thus, one who is well-versed in the scriptures chants along; whether the deposit of words is fewer or the deposit of the well-versed one consists of nine words, the chanting is more extensive than the [original] brief statement.
This is called both the Chanting and the Investigation; this is the Mode of Conveying Investigation.
In that regard, what is the Mode of Conveying Reasoning?
“Of all the Modes of Conveying...”
“The plane and the range of these, as well as the investigation of their fitness and unfitness—
this is explained as the Mode of Conveying the Method.”
The teaching regarding the sixteen strings, the analysis thereof, and that which is demonstrated—this is the demonstration (*niddesa*).
The inquiry as to whether this question is not applicable to the suttas—this is the reasoning (*yutti*).

For instance: beings become defiled with causes and conditions; there is a cause, there is a condition for the defilement of beings. Beings become purified with causes and conditions; there is a cause, there is a condition for the purification of beings.

“Ānanda, a person endowed with virtue need not declare: ‘How might remorse arise in me? … [as before] … non-declaration should be made; this is the path to purification. What is its cause and condition?
For the aggregate of virtue, there are four causes and four conditions.
Association with superior persons and dwelling in a suitable locality—this is the state of being conditioned by a proximate cause, which possesses a condition.”
Whatever past karma constitutes the condition for its ripening, the right application of self through that condition is the cause.
Thus, the aggregate of virtue is "with cause and with condition"—this refers to mundane virtue.
As for supramundane virtue, however, three faculties are its condition.
The faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, and the faculty of concentration—
this is the condition.
The faculty of mindfulness and the faculty of wisdom are the cause.
The virtue that arises through wisdom leading to penetration is the cause and the condition for the virtue of a stream-enterer.
Furthermore, serenity, rapture, and gladness are the conditions for concentration.
That happiness which is the cause: by that, the aggregate of concentration has a cause and a condition.
That which one who is concentrated understands as it really is, is wisdom.

For that [wisdom], the voice of another and wise attention internally are the cause and the condition. Thus these three aggregates have causes and conditions; in this way, there are seven kinds of wisdom.
And it is not consistent with the suttas that provide sevenfold explanations.
This is the Mode of Conveying the Logical.
It is to be seen within the four Great Authorities (*mahāpadesa*).
In this regard, what is the proximate cause?
"The Victor teaches the Dhamma,
and that which is the proximate cause of that Dhamma..."
"Thus, up to all phenomena—
this is the Mode of Conveying the Footing.
In this context, the five strands of sensual pleasure are the footing for sensual lust.

In whomever sensual lust arises—whether it has arisen, is arising, or will arise—it does so with reference to these five forms as sense bases, and not apart from them; this is the proximate cause for sensual lust.
Therefore, it is said that the five strands of sensual pleasure are the proximate cause for sensual lust.
The five faculties are the proximate cause for lust for form.
The faculty of mind is the proximate cause for lust for existence.
The five aggregates are the proximate cause for the view of a personal body.
The sixty-one types of speculative views are the proximate cause for lust for views.
The sense-sphere realm (kāmadhātu) is the proximate cause for sensual lust (kāmarāga).
The formless realm (arūpadhātu) is the proximate cause for formless lust (arūparāga).
The perception of pleasure (sukhasaññā) is the proximate cause for sensual lust.
The perception of ill will is the proximate cause for ill will.
Lack of clear comprehension is the proximate cause for confusion.
The nine grounds for resentment are the proximate cause for ill will.
The ninefold conceit is the proximate cause for conceit.
Pleasant feeling is the proximate cause for the underlying tendency to lust.
Painful feeling is the proximate cause for the underlying tendency to aversion.
Neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is the proximate cause for the underlying tendency to ignorance.
Clinging to a self-doctrine and false speech are the proximate causes for greed.
Killing living beings, malicious speech, and harsh speech are the proximate causes for ill will.
Wrong view and idle chatter are the footing for delusion.
Existence and wealth are the footing for the conceit "I am.
Possessiveness toward external things is the footing for the conceit "mine."
Attachment to the body is the proximate cause for wrong view.
Bodily fault is the proximate cause for hatred.
Bodily impurity is the proximate cause for greed.

Whatever state arises by means of whatever object—whether through a foundation of truth, a foundation of phenomena, or through underlying tendencies—that phenomenon is its proximate cause (*padatthāna*).
By means of that object, that phenomenon arises.
Just as a person, failing to find a foothold for his first step, lifts his second foot and then brings it down behind the other.
But if that which does not serve as the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) for the second term extracts another term,
and that [other term] becomes its condition—
thus, whether a phenomenon (*dhamma*) be wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate, it does not proceed if it fails to obtain its proximate cause.
The acquisition of the source for a state that has been expounded—this is called the Mode of Conveying the Footing (padaṭṭhāna-hāra).
In this regard, what is the Mode of Conveying Characteristics (lakkhaṇa-hāra)?
"When a single state has been spoken..."
"Those phenomena which have a single characteristic—
all these are said by him [the Buddha];
that method is called the 'Characteristic' (lakkhaṇa) mode."

Regarding the verse beginning, "For those by whom mindfulness directed to the body (*kāyagatāsati*) is well undertaken," it is said that mindfulness directed to the body, mindfulness directed to feelings, mindfulness directed to the mind, and mindfulness directed to mental phenomena are included within one of the four foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*).

For the mind does not proceed in only a single station of consciousness; it proceeds through various destinations. Thus, what was stated regarding mindfulness directed to the body is also stated for mindfulness directed to feelings, the mind, and mental phenomena.
Indeed, when mindfulness directed to the body is developed, the four foundations of mindfulness do not fail to reach the perfection of development.
Thus, when such categories of phenomena have been stated, all phenomena have been stated.
In the verse, “The purification of one’s own mind—this is the teaching of the Buddhas,” mental factors (*cetasika*) are stated, and form (*rūpa*) is stated in relation to the mind.
This is name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the Noble Truth of Suffering.
Then, regarding the purification of one's own mind: that which is purified is suffering;
that by which it is purified is the path;
and that from which the purification arises is cessation.

Dependent upon the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises; there, the co-nascent feeling, perception, volition, contact, and attention—these phenomena have a single characteristic by way of the characteristic of arising.
One who becomes disenchanted with form becomes disenchanted with feeling, and one becomes disenchanted with perception, formations, and consciousness as well.

Thus, when one phenomenon among those phenomena that have a single characteristic has been demonstrated, all phenomena are demonstrated. This is called the Mode of Conveying Characteristics (*lakkhaṇo hāro*).
In this regard, what is the fourfold method of analysis (catubyūha-hāra)?
“The phrasing, the intention, the syllables, and the teaching;”
“The meaning of the sutta is the connection between what precedes and what follows;
this is the fourfold method.
In that regard, what is “language” (nirutti), and how is it to be sought?
As it was said by the Blessed One: “A bhikkhu endowed with eleven factors quickly attains greatness among the teachings;

he is skilled in the meaning, skilled in the Dhamma, skilled in language, skilled in the designations for women, skilled in the designations for men, skilled in the designations for neuter beings, and skilled in the designations for the past.”

He is skilled in the designation of the past, skilled in the designation of the future, and skilled in the designation of the present. He is skilled in a single intention and skilled in various intentions.
In what has it been taught? In the past, the future, and the present.
By means of the designations for women, the designations for men, and the designations for persons, everything has been demonstrated in accordance with the Sutta.
One who examines, from the perspective of the phrasing and skill in terminology, whether a particular passage in the Sutta is well-expressed or poorly expressed, should apply this [method] thus:
"This too should not be applied."
This is called skill in language.
In this context, what is skill in the underlying intention (*adhippāya*)?
It is knowing that the entire discourse as it was taught by the Blessed One follows a specific sequence, such that "this is what ought to have been taught by the Blessed One [at this point]."
"What is it that the deathless state is heedfulness, and the state of death is heedlessness?"—this is the verse.
What is the Blessed One’s intention here?
His intention is this: those who desire even [the attainment of] the eighty [great qualities] will dwell heedfully.
The time for yoga does not turn back for one who practices it; there, no evils arise for him.
This has been proclaimed by the seeker of the path of feeling.
"Those whose dust and impurities have been shaken off are liberated from suffering.
What is the Blessed One’s intention here? It is this:
those who find no gratification in suffering will arouse energy for the destruction of suffering.
This is the Blessed One’s intended meaning (adhippāya) therein.

Thus, whether taught by means of a verse or an exposition, it is established by this sutta that "he who practices in accordance with the Dhamma" is the intended meaning; this is called the intended meaning of the teaching (desanādhippāya).
In this regard, what is the connection between what precedes and what follows (pubbāparasandhi)?

Whatever verses there are in this [work] or in the discourses, they number eighty; these are "thus" or "in this way. Whatever the preceding words and whatever the subsequent words of that verse or discourse are, they must be brought together.
In this way, the connection between what precedes and what follows is understood.
When a single verse has been undertaken, or two or three, if the meaning of those spoken in one part remains unindicated by other verses—whether spoken or unspoken—that must be investigated.
Whatever investigation there may be for one who is thus searching, or whatever further things to be sought among the designations of that person—
this is called the connection between what precedes and what follows.
Skillfulness means skillfulness regarding the basis and the cause.
Skill in language through the phrasing;
skill in the intention behind the teaching;
and skill in the underlying connection between what precedes and what follows.
In that regard, the verse or the introductory narrative (nidāna) for it has been sought.

There is no need to point out [the meaning] from the basis (vatthu) if it is not found; rather, skill in the source (nidāna-kosalla) and skill in the meaning (attha-kosalla) consist in the meaning being sought as it truly is through these four terms.

Furthermore, whatever intention, phrasing, language, and connection exists—whether from the basis or from the source—that unsurpassed [meaning] is to be taught according to the sequence of what precedes and follows in this way, by means of the meaning of the discourse (suttattha).
This is the fourfold method of exposition (*catubyūha-hāra*).
In that regard, what is the method of turning back (*āvaṭṭa-hāra*)?
"In a single footing..."
One seeks the remaining footing;
it turns back toward the opposite side—
this is the Mode of Conveying Turning Back (Āvaṭṭa-hāra).
As in the verses beginning, "Of those who are arrogant and heedless...
What is the proximate cause of heedlessness?
It is the neglect of wholesome states.
But what is the proximate cause for the excellence of wholesome states?
It is the cultivation of unwholesome states.
And what is the proximate cause for that? It is the cultivation of wholesome states.
What is the proximate cause for the indulgence in the basis of the defilements?
Thus, through negligence, there is the view belonging to delusion and ignorance, which belongs to the side of desire and lust.
In that regard, craving and views constitute the four taints: the taint of craving, the taint of existence, the taint of views, and the taint of ignorance.

In this context, the view that "it exists" regarding the mind and "it is permanent" regarding mental factors constitutes the taint of views (*diṭṭhāsava*). The taint of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*) arises from indulging in the five strands of sensual pleasure; the taint of existence (*bhavāsava*) arises from attachment to rebirths.
Therein, the material body (*rūpakāya*) is the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) for both the taint of sensual desire and the taint of existence.
The mental body (*nāmakāya*) is the proximate cause for the taint of views and the taint of ignorance (*avijjāsava*).
In this context, clinging and inward driving are the characteristic of the taint of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*).

Aspiration, bondage, and the volitional formation of the body are the characteristic of the taint of existence (*bhavāsava*). Misapprehension and dogmatic adherence are the characteristic of the taint of views (*diṭṭhāsava*).
Non-penetration and lack of clear comprehension regarding phenomena are the characteristic of the taint of ignorance (*avijjāsava*).

These four taints are the four clingings: the taint of sensual desire is clinging to sensual pleasures; the taint of existence is clinging to existence; the taint of views is clinging to views; and the taint of ignorance is clinging to a doctrine of self. Through these four clingings, there are the five aggregates.
Among them, the taint of ignorance is to be abandoned in the mind; it is abandoned by one who contemplates the mind as mind.
The taint of views is to be abandoned among phenomena; it is abandoned by one who contemplates phenomena as phenomena.
The taint of existence is to be abandoned through attachment; it is abandoned by one who contemplates feelings as feelings.
The taint of sensual desire is to be abandoned among the five strands of sensual pleasure; it is abandoned by one who contemplates the body as the body.
In this context, contemplation of the body pertains to the Noble Truth of Suffering (*dukkha-ariyasacca*).

Contemplation of feelings is a condition for the five faculties—the faculty of pleasure, the faculty of pain, the faculty of mental joy, the faculty of mental grief, and the faculty of equanimity—and because it involves the approach of the seven defilements, it pertains to the Origin (*samudaya*).
Contemplation of the mind within the mind pertains to Cessation (*nirodha*).
Contemplation of phenomena among phenomena partakes of the Path.

Therefore, through that very vision regarding the four [noble truths], all those [defilements] are abandoned by him; whereas for those previously described as arrogant and negligent, their taints increase.
For one who knows and sees, there is the destruction of the taints; for the unwholesome phenomena are indeed suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
Thus they are to be sought.
As far as the destination of that unwholesome state extends, one seeks unwholesome phenomena by way of their opposite; thus one turns back from those defilements.
This is called the Mode of Conveying Turning Back (āvaṭṭa-hāra).
In this way, bright qualities too are to be sought.
They will follow upon unwholesome qualities.

In this context, this is the ground for the Mode of Conveying a Conversion: mindfulness, the foundations [of mindfulness], the perversions, the four kinds of knowledge, the practice leading to the origination of identity, and the practice leading to the cessation of identity.
In this context, what is the Mode of Conveying Analysis (vibhatti-hāra)?
Whatever is to be explained by way of analysis is called the Mode of Conveying Analysis.

For example: "Having come, how does a person become [such] again? or "He does not revile what has been said," or "By means of inquiry and questioning, he goes beyond the question for the sake of one person. Such is [the Mode of Conveying Analysis].
This is called the Mode of Conveying Analysis (vibhatti-hāra).
Therein, what is the Mode of Conveying Reversal (parivattana-hāra)?
Whatever is a description of an opposite [quality], this is called the Mode of Conveying Reversal.
As it was said by the Blessed One: "For a person of right view, wrong view is worn away," and so on in detail for all the factors of the path.
This is called the Mode of Conveying Reversal (*parivattano hāro*).
In this regard, what is the Mode of Conveying Synonyms (*vevacano hāro*)?
“By means of many synonyms,
a single Dhamma is proclaimed;
he who knows this in the Sutta is a knower of the Suttas.”
“That is the Mode of Conveying Synonyms (vevacana-hāra).

For example, the Venerable Sāriputta was praised by the Blessed One in a single instance through various synonyms as ‘Sāriputta is of great wisdom, of laughing wisdom, of swift wisdom’—this is a synonym for wisdom.
And likewise, in the *Maggavibhaṅga*, the meaning of ‘leading out’ (niyyāna) is demonstrated for each individual path-factor through its synonyms.”
Such are the synonyms for ignorance (*avijjā*).
It is a single unwholesome root, yet being that very same thing, people in various regions understand it by various names.
For they do not even speak of it by its own name, but rather resort to another term.
"Of the bhikkhu who has abandoned all sensual desires"—here "sensual desires" (kāmā) is what is being addressed.
"For whom the flood has been crossed"—he addresses those very same sensual desires as the "flood" (saṅka).
"While hearing [the teaching], they first become excited"—he addresses those very same sensual desires as "excited" (rajjanti).
Thus, regarding the teaching given in a sutta, the investigation of it is as follows: "Of which dhamma is this the name?
Of which is this a synonym? For the Omniscient One teaches by whatever linguistic expression (nirutti) is appropriate for each person; therefore, its synonyms must be investigated.
This is the Mode of Conveying Synonyms (Vevacanahāra).
In this context, what is the mode of conveying through description (paññatti-hāra)?
It points to the discourse: "The four noble truths. This is the description by way of formal presentation (nikkhepa-paññatti).
It is the description of the origin [of suffering].
As long as there is desire for physical nutriment, there is lust, up to its establishment.
Therein, consciousness is described by way of manifestation through origination.
When there is no desire for physical nutriment … [etc. … it is described by way of eradication.

"His mind is liberated from the taint of sensual desire, his mind is liberated from the taint of existence, and his mind is liberated from the taint of ignorance"—thus he proclaims the designation of abandonment.
"He whose craving is set aside, whose wisdom revolves"—this verse proclaims the designation of what is agreeable.
In this way, the Blessed One proclaims a single dhamma as the designation of what is agreeable.
For craving is not established as the origin of suffering by having craving demonstrated as the origin in every instance.
Just as there is a "description by way of rejection" when one does not tolerate, but dispels and abandons, a sensual thought as it arises,
so too, regarding all phenomena— both wholesome and unwholesome— that which constitutes his field of phenomena, that very phenomenon occurs therein.
The remaining phenomena are dependent upon it.
That designation (paññatti) is twofold:
dependent designation (parādhīna-paññatti) and self-dependent designation (sādhīna-paññatti).
What is dependent designation?
"Monks, develop concentration; for a monk who is concentrated, monks, understands things as they really are.

He understands as it really is: 'Form is impermanent. This is both dependent designation and other-dependent designation; that designation belongs to both wisdom and virtue, just as one should develop the four jhānas.

In him, the faculty of concentration is weak while the other four faculties are dependent; those three forms of confirmed confidence (*aveccappasāda*) are dependent, as is the faculty of concentration, and these four faculties are dependent.

However, among the four noble truths, the faculty of wisdom (*paññindriya*) is independent, and among the foundations of mindfulness and the right efforts, the faculty of energy (*vīriyindriya*) is independent.
Thus, that Dhamma is dependent upon its own proximate cause and its own field; and it is to be described therein.
Its opposition and suppression must be demonstrated.
Herein, this description in many ways [addresses] the question: "For what reason is this Dhamma described?"
This is called description.
In this context, what is the method of entry?
It is to be applied to six things.
In which six?
In the aggregates, the elements, the sense bases, the faculties, the truths, and dependent origination.
There is no discourse, verse, or exposition that is not included therein.
He does not appear in any one of these six states.

To this extent, all that teaching—whether it be the aggregates (*khandha*), the elements (*dhātu*), the sense bases (*āyatana*), the truths (*sacca*), or dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*)—is covered. Therein, among the five aggregates, the aggregate of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*) is the proximate cause for lust, hatred, and delusion.

Therein, regarding the three types of feeling: in the case of pleasant feeling, he is joyful and possessed of sustained thought (*savicāra*); in the case of painful feeling, he is grieved and possessed of sustained thought; in the case of neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he is equanimous and possessed of sustained thought.
Furthermore, whatever is felt therein is the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*). Among the aggregates, it is the aggregate of formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*);

therein, the body proceeds heedlessly along with its underlying tendencies. And that which belongs to formations is twofold: the crossing over of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) through karma, and the three types of formations—meritorious, non-meritorious, or imperturbable—which are the cause for one who is still possessed of lust, but not for one who is free from lust.
One who is not free from lust intends and plans the formative activities of hatred; however, one who is free from lust intends but does not plan them.
Just as a hot thunderbolt, falling upon wood, a tree, or elsewhere, both shatters and burns it, so too does volition accompanied by lust both intend and plan.
Just as a diamond does not break or burn those who possess it, so too the volition of one free from lust intends and does not form [new karma].
In that regard, among the five aggregates, one aggregate—the aggregate of perception—is the body without faculties.
In that regard, among the elements, there are eighteen elements.
In that context, when the ten material elements are being taught, the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*) is to be demonstrated; this is the Noble Truth of Suffering (*dukkha-ariyasacca*).

Furthermore, as for the six bodies of consciousness with the mind-element as the seventh, there the aggregate of consciousness (*viññāṇakkhandha*) is to be demonstrated; this is the Noble Truth of Suffering.

However, the mental-object element (*dhammadhātu*) is a convergence of phenomena (*dhammasamosaraṇā*); that phenomenon is to be demonstrated by whatever means it is apprehended—whether by way of cause, outflow, fruit, function, or synonym.
Whether they be wholesome, unwholesome, indeterminate, or unconditioned:
among the twelve bases, ten bases are material form; that is to be pointed out as the Noble Truth of Suffering.
The aggregate of form and the mind-base are to be pointed out by means of the aggregate of consciousness as the Noble Truth of Suffering.
The base of mental phenomena is the convergence of various phenomena.

Therein, those phenomena that pertain to the faculties should be demonstrated among the faculties, and those that do not pertain to the faculties should be demonstrated among those that are not faculties.
They should also be applied according to the method of exposition.
Just as that element of phenomena (dhammadhātu) is, so should the sphere of phenomena (dhammāyatana) be sought.
For the element of phenomena is indeed the same as the sphere of phenomena—neither less nor more.
In this regard, dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) is threefold, it is fourfold, and it is twofold.
In this regard, dependent origination is threefold: cause, condition, and result.

Ignorance, volitional formations, craving, and clinging—these are the cause. Consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling—these are the condition. Existence is the result; birth and aging-and-death are the outcome.
How is it fourfold: cause, condition, result, and outcome? [As described above.]
Ignorance, craving, volitional formations, and clinging—
this is the cause.
Consciousness is the condition for name-and-form.
Name-and-form arises; for one thus arisen, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling occur—this is the condition.
That which is existence is this result.
Whatever is birth and whatever is aging and death—
this is the outcome.
How is dependent origination twofold?
Ignorance, volitional formations, craving, and clinging— this is the origin.
Consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, existence, birth, and aging-and-death— [this is the cessation].
"This is suffering.
Furthermore, "with the cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of volitional formations"—these two truths are presented by way of their respective opposites.
Therefore, dependent origination should be demonstrated in whatever manner it has been demonstrated.
Likewise, there are twenty-two faculties.
Twelve faculties are the eye-faculty and so forth, up to the grief-faculty; this is suffering.
Furthermore, the male faculty and the view-faculty are the footing for craving.
Since a man must act in this way toward other men, he then becomes infatuated with what is internal. This is the conceit of "I" (*ahaṅkāra*);

being enamored by that fame, he searches externally, thinking, "This is mine" (*mamaṅkāra*); thus, in regard to a woman, the faculty of pleasure (*sukhindriya*) and the faculty of mental joy (*somanassindriya*) become followers of the male faculty (*purisindriya*).
When his intention is fulfilled, states of greed increase within his roots of the wholesome.
But if this intention of his does not reach fulfillment,
then the faculty of pain and the faculty of mental grief arise in him.
And hatred, which is a root of unwholesomeness,
increases. But if one develops equanimity, one becomes compliant with the faculty of equanimity,
and non-delusion, which is a root of wholesomeness, increases.
Thus, these seven faculties—namely, all feeling, the femininity faculty, and the masculinity faculty—are not to be pursued and are inferior when based upon the ground of defilement.
Therein, the eight faculties—from the faith faculty up to the faculty of one who has already known—constitute the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
For the ten types of wisdom-faculty, sensual lust is the proximate cause.
The faculty of mind is the proximate cause for lust for existence.
The faculties of wisdom are the proximate cause for lust for form.
The female faculty and the male faculty are the proximate cause for the designation of a being.
In that regard, by whichever faculty one is able to bring a verse down for application, it should be demonstrated by means of that very faculty.
Thus, among the aggregates, elements, bases, truths, and dependent origination, this is the Mode of Conveying Descent.
In that regard, what is the Mode of Conveying Purification?
Regarding those who will recite the verses beginning with one:
when one has been recited, the meaning should not yet be demonstrated while the remaining ones are still to be recited.
What is the reason?
For that meaning has not yet been spoken; what has not been spoken cannot be pointed out. How so?
It is like the verse, “Heedfulness is the path to the Deathless. This single verse must be pointed out.
What is the reason? Because this undertaking has not yet been spoken of.
“Having thus understood this distinction,
the wise take delight in heedfulness; they rejoice in heedfulness.”
"He delights in the range of the noble ones.
This has been spoken.
The meaning of this verse that has been spoken must now be demonstrated.
"What is the reason? Is there anything remaining there?
[The answer is: "Those meditators are constant, always firm in their exertion"—this verse. When these verses have been thus examined, then the meaning should be demonstrated.
Thus has a single recitation been spoken regarding discourses or explanations never heard before.
Whatever investigation and weighing there is— namely, whether this is a duty, this is a discourse spoken, or whether its synonym has been demonstrated or not—
that investigation therein is called the Mode of Conveying Purification (Sodhana-hāra).
In that regard, what is the Mode of Conveying Determination (Adhiṭṭhāna-hāra)?
There is unity and diversity.
In this regard, there is the designation of the state and the designation of the function.

That unity and diversity, according to how they are designated—by means of a single synonym one understands diversity—is wisdom (*paññā*); and that [wisdom] is a designation in the sense of predominance (*ādhipateyya*).
That which is designated in the sense of being incomparable is the power of wisdom (*paññābala*) in the sense of being incomparable.

It dwells upon the three jewels— the recollection of the Buddha, the recollection of the Dhamma, and the recollection of the Saṅgha— by way of their being its domain, having become attenuated through the power of [its] cultivation, because it is a non-perverted recollection.
Right view is the investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor through the discernment of phenomena; it is higher knowledge by way of directing. In brief, what are the paths?

They are a single entity because they do not disturb their respective bases, just as water mixed with heat is "hot water" and water mixed with cold is "cold water," or as alkaline water and sugared water. This is unity and diversity.
Furthermore, there is a phenomenon composed of various phenomena that is one, such as form which consists of four [elements] to be restrained; that is form—this is unity.
The earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element: this is their diversity (*vemattatā*).
Thus, all four elements are "form" (*rūpa*): this is their unity (*ekattatā*); yet they are diverse as the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element.
As for the earth element, it is a unity by way of its characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*), but it is diverse by way of its various locations (*saṅkiṇṇavatthu*).
Whatever has the characteristic of hardness, all that is the earth element: this is unity.
Hair of the head, hair of the body, nails, teeth, skin, and hide: these are diversity.
Thus, all four elements are "form" (rūpa): this is unity.
Sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles are diversity.
Furthermore, there is a state that is a diversity and receives another name:
namely, the nine perceptions in the contemplation of the body—the perception of the livid, the perception of the bloated—this is the perception of foulness (*asubhasaññā*).

That which is unity in terms of the object and diversity in terms of the mental aspect—this is, for one who thus perceives the danger in perceptions and feelings, the concentration faculty with such a basis;
this very thing is the development of perception regarding phenomena therein, as well as the energy faculty, which is the contemplation of phenomena regarding phenomena;
and it is the wisdom faculty, which is the contemplation of mind in one who abandons the perception of self regarding the mind.

Thus, whatever range of knowledge there is, which is entirely the domain of wisdom—that is wisdom; this is its diversity. Just as there is diversity in craving, such as sensual lust, lust for existence, and lust for views, so too is there diversity here.
Thus, the knowledge, investigation, and weighing that occur through both unity and diversity—this is the Mode of Conveying the Foundation.
In this context, what is the Mode of Conveying Requisites (*parikkhāra-hāra*)?
Purification and defilement, together with their causes and conditions—that investigation of both is the Mode of Conveying Requisites.
Thus, for phenomena that have causes, the cause must be investigated; for those that have conditions, the condition must be investigated.
In this regard, what is the difference between a cause (*hetu*) and a condition (*paccaya*)?
A cause is intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*); a condition is extrinsic nature (*parabhāva*).

An extrinsic nature is both a condition and a cause; however, regarding intrinsic nature, that which is a cause for extrinsic nature is not called a "cause" but is called a "condition. When it is stated as a cause, it is a cause; when it is stated as a condition, it is a condition.
The internal is the cause; the external is the condition.
The intrinsic nature is the cause; the extrinsic nature is the condition.
That which produces is the cause; that which receives is the condition.
The resident is the cause; the visitor is the condition.
The unique is the cause; the common is the condition.
The cause is singular; the condition is successive.
The equipment for the cause must be procured.
Procurement is the cause; therein, the cause is twofold.
The condition is twofold.
There is the immediate condition and the remote condition.
Cause is also twofold:
the immediate cause and the remote cause.
In this context, what is the remote condition (*paramparapaccaya*)?
Ignorance (*avijjā*) is the remote condition for name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); consciousness (*viññāṇa*) is a condition by way of being the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapaccayatā*).
If, at the beginning, there is the cessation of ignorance, there is also the cessation of name-and-form.

In this context, what is the reason? The "immediate condition" (*samanantara-paccaya*) is derived from the "successive condition" (*parampara-paccaya*). This is [the classification] by way of condition.
In that regard, what is the successive cause (*paramparahetu*)?
For one who cognizes, it is a cause by way of being a successive cause; for another aspect, it is a cause by way of being an immediate cause (*samanantara-hetu*).

For whatever arises immediately after something else, that [latter] is the cause of the former. Through the cessation of birth, there is the cessation of appearance; through the cessation of appearance, the cessation of the staff;
through the cessation of the staff, the cessation of the fragment. Thus, that cause should be seen in two ways by those [who see].
Just as ignorance is a condition for dependent origination, what is its condition in turn? It is improper attention (*ayoniso manasikāra*).
Thus, for what are the formations the condition? In this way, both the condition and that which has arisen—what is their cause? It is ignorance alone.
For indeed, no prior limit is discerned.

Therein, the underlying tendency to ignorance is the cause of the manifestation of ignorance; the former is the cause and the latter is the condition, and that ignorance is also [the cause] of the formations.
The condition [of ignorance] is by way of four reasons: as a conascence-condition, as a contiguity-condition, as a suffusion-condition, and as a foundation-condition.
How is it a condition for volitional formations by way of being a conascence-condition?
When the mind is obsessed by lust, there, through the obsession of ignorance, it destroys the entire range of wisdom.

Therein, formations—having the three conditions as their basis and belonging to the stages of the temporal process—attain growth, increase, and abundance arising from that very ignorance; thus, wisdom is abandoned for four reasons.
What are the four?
Latent tendency (*anusaya*), obsession (*pariyuṭṭhāna*), fetter (*saṁyojana*), and clinging (*upādāna*).
Therein, the latent tendency is the obsession; when one is obsessed, one is fettered; being fettered, one clings; and with clinging as condition, there is becoming (*bhava*).
Thus those threefold formations have arisen and reached the plane [of existence], yet they do not lead to non-perishing; this is because they have been disciplined by the Path.
When these have become established and are no longer easily dispelled, they are also called "formations. Thus, in the sense of being arisen with a cause, there exists a condition for formations;

having set aside what has been demonstrated [as the specific condition], one should include the wholesome, the unwholesome, and that which is both wholesome and unwholesome, and having set aside those things subject to result (vipākadhamma), one should speak of the expressible, the inexpressible, and that which is both expressible and inexpressible.
It should be inserted; it should be surrounded by the *bhavāpeviritta* and all the sutta.

The ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, merits, and the unshared [qualities]—ignorance is a condition for volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*) by way of immediate condition (*samanantara-paccaya*).
Ignorance that has arisen together with whatever mind is the immediately preceding mind of that mind.

Regarding "arisen together": when that immediately preceding consciousness has arisen, the preceding consciousness is a condition for the succeeding consciousness by way of being a root-condition (*hetu-paccaya*).
Because of that, ignorance is the cause; because of that consciousness, clinging arises and knowledge does not arise due to the lack of opportunity provided.
That element of his which, through heedlessness, is permeated by covetousness—therein arise the perversions [of perception]: "the beautiful in the ugly" and "pleasure in the painful.
Therein, formations arise; being lustful and corrupt, the volition rooted therein arises through the obsession of lust, the obsession of ill-will, and the obsession of ignorance.
This perversion of view is to be demonstrated in the exposition of the basis.
That which one cognizes with a perverted mind is the perversion of mind; that perverted perception which grasps is the perversion of perception;
that perverted view which adheres is the perversion of view.
The eight wrongnesses increase, and the three unwholesome states—along with consciousness and ignorance arising from improper attention—bring them about.
Thus, in the past and future, unwholesome formations increase and reach abundance.
And these formations, which lead to renewed existence, remain largely unrecognized.
Thus, ignorance is a condition for formations by way of being a co-nascent condition and by way of being an immediately preceding condition.
In what way is ignorance a condition for volitional formations by way of soaking them?
That ignorance soaks and permeates those volitional formations.
Just as, for example, a blue lotus or a red lotus, growing in water, reaches growth, increase, development, and abundance because it is soaked and saturated with cool water.
Thus, ignorance is a condition for volitional formations in the sense of moistening.
How is ignorance a condition for volitional formations in the sense of establishing?
Those volitional formations reach growth, increase, and abundance by depending upon ignorance.
Just as a blue lotus, a red lotus, or a white lotus, depending on the earth and established upon the earth, attains growth, increase, and abundance;
so too these formations, established in ignorance and depending on ignorance, go to growth, increase, and abundance.
Thus, in the sense of being a basis, ignorance is the condition for formations.
Furthermore, through the ripening of karma accompanied by lust, existence (*bhava*) arises at rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*);

because that entire [existence] is clung to through ignorance, it is called "formations leading to renewed existence" (*ponobhavikā saṅkhārā*). Thus, too, there are formations conditioned by ignorance.

Furthermore, among the five types of persons—those who are trainees (*sekkhā*), those who have attained the attainment of non-perception (*asaññisamāpatti*), and those who have reached the peak of existence (*bhavagata*)—[the formations exist].

And as for those born by moisture (*saṃsedaja*) who are already included therein, or anyone else who has become a non-returner (*anāgāmin*)—who neither wills nor aspires—by what conditions do their volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*) arise?

Furthermore, there exists in them passion (*rāga*); their volitional formations and grasping (*upādāna*) continue to follow the mind, being unextinguished because their ripening (*vipāka*) is not yet matured, and their conditions (*paccaya*) are not severed; thus, they go back again to existence.
For in this way, too, there are volitional formations conditioned by ignorance.

Furthermore, those [volitional formations] are neither clinging nor volitional formations; rather, it is because their seven underlying tendencies have not been eradicated and have not been cut off that they become the object for that [consciousness].
With consciousness established, there is name-and-form conditioned by consciousness.
Thus, too, with ignorance as condition, there are volitional formations.
Furthermore, whatever karma leads to accumulation is all conditioned by way of ignorance, adhered to by way of craving, and through lack of knowledge one does not perceive the danger therein.
That itself becomes the seed of consciousness; that itself becomes the moisture of craving.
That very ignorance is delusion.
In this way too, it can be said that formations have ignorance as their condition.
Thus, by these modes, ignorance is the condition for formations.
Therein, improper attention is the cause of ignorance and its condition.
Therein, this interruption is the third power; cessation occurs there, and this is rebirth-linking.
Therein, renewed existence is that which is uninterrupted; in the sense of not being eradicated, it is the underlying tendency (*anusaya*).
Just as when two people squeeze a cloth or a garment, one or both might press it, yet they would not dry it by squeezing;
in that case, the moisture-element (*āpodhātu*) adhering to it must be dried by means of heat.

If, having applied the element of heat, one were to place it back in the air, it would become mostly moist again through evaporation; for it would not reach total exhaustion without the arrival of the fire-element (*tejodhātu*).
In the same way, even the attainment that has the peak of existence as its limit does not lead to the eradication of what is appropriate.
For they cling to it and contemplate it, yet they do not proceed from craving to the abandoning of craving.
In that case, there is no eradication.
The underlying tendency (*anusaya*) toward ignorance and its obstruction of the mind—this is the obsession (*pariyuṭṭhāna*).
The non-penetration of consciousness as it really is is this taint of ignorance (*avijjāsava*), which becomes the seed of consciousness for becoming (*avijjā-viññāṇa-bīja*).
That which is the seed is the cause; it is not cut off. Being uncut, it links up [to a new existence].
One who is reconnecting does not undergo eradication.
When the mind is not eradicated, it becomes enveloped; one whose mind is enveloped does not understand things as they truly are.

Thus, for recognition, there is the sense of being subject to taints, the sense of ignorance, the sense of cause, the sense of non-interruption, the sense of non-retrogression, and the sense of fruit.
The meaning of rebirth-linking, the meaning of renewed existence, the meaning of non-eradication, the meaning of underlying tendency, the meaning of obsession, and the meaning of non-penetration.
To this extent the field of ignorance is demonstrated.
This is called the Mode of Conveying Requisites.
In this context, what is the Mode of Conveying Coordination?
When something has been grasped in brief, it should be stated in detail as it truly is.
For those who know the mind according to its detailed classification, this is the Mode of Conveying Coordination.

In this context, the "designation by name" (*nāmaniddesa*) is the brief summary (*upaghaṭaka*), while the "designation of the basis" (*vatthuniddesa*) is the synonym and constitutes the detailed exposition (*vitthāra*).
What is it like? That which is to be abandoned by monks through proper conduct is the "brief summary.
In that regard, what is the "synthesis" (*samāropana*)?
Nothing need be said [here], or rather, the lust for form (*rūparāga*) should be abandoned along with the mind-base (*nāmavat*).
This should be expanded in detail up to consciousness (*viññāṇa*).
Ignorance (*avijjā*) should be made known by means of a simile; this is the application (*samāropana*).
For one whose mind is dependent, there are two kinds of dependence: craving and views.
Therein, views are ignorance and craving is volitional formations.
Therein, with views as condition there is craving; these are volitional formations with ignorance as condition.
Therein, consciousness dependent [on a basis]—this is "consciousness conditioned by volitional formations" up to old age and death. When this has been stated in brief, it completes what remains.
For one who thinks, "There is no movement for that which is non-dependent," there is the abandoning of both views and craving.
Therein, through the cessation of view and ignorance, consciousness—which is real—approaches various phenomena that are conducive to lust and runs toward other phenomena.
By way of the simile of the monkey, he has no desire or lust for inferior things that are provocative of passion;
how then could there be any wavering from them? His mind will be directed toward superior beings; that consciousness, being unsupported, ceases for lack of nutriment.
With the cessation of consciousness comes the cessation of name-and-form, and so on, up to the cessation of aging and death.
This is the coordination.
In this context, the movement of consciousness by way of lust is accompanied by grasping; when that movement is absent, the threefold fire of the conventional usage of "affliction" becomes subsided.
Therefore he said: "When there is no movement, there is tranquility."
In that regard, through the application [of the factors], one whose body is tranquil experiences happiness;
the mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated, until there arises the knowledge and vision: "Liberation has been attained.
Through the destruction of the taints, he attains liberation and is not reborn.
"Because for that rebirth there is no coming or going, neither here nor beyond, nor in between the two—'this indeed is the end of suffering,'" this is the element of Nibbāna without residue.
This is what has been superimposed in the middle of this sutta regarding both dependent origination and liberation; yet they do not analyze in detail the meaning of what was spoken by him in brief.
This is called the Mode of Conveying Coordination (*samāropano hāro*).

It is not by means of a discourse dealing with defilement (*saṅkilesabhāgiya*) that those phenomena which are to be coordinated with a discourse dealing with defilement are coordinated, nor any others.
The same applies to discourses dealing with purification (*vāsanābhāgiya*) and penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiya*); this is the Mode of Conveying Coordination.
These are the sixteen strings.
This is the fifth stage, called the Analysis of the Strings, in the *Peṭakopadesa* of Mahākaccāyana, the son of Suvīra, who dwelt in the Rose-apple Grove.
